content:
The initial stage of AI coding was vibe coding: You write the prompts, AI writes the code, you review it. Your role was basically a writer.

Then we moved to agentic engineering, which is where most of us are now. You orchestrate multiple agents doing multiple things simultaneously, and your role shifted to director.

Auto-research represents the next jump. You define a goal, hand over a metric and an assessment method, and the agents run completely autonomously. You set the direction, but you're no longer directing individual tasks. Your role is more like a principal investigator at a research lab—you tell the RAs what to investigate and they go run the experiments.

I think what comes after that is each of us becoming the CEO of our own company, whether it's a real company or just the way we organize our personal productivity. You'll have fleets of agents running constantly on your behalf, optimizing things, handling tasks, making small decisions—and your job is just to set the vision and course-correct when needed.

To make a long story short, this is a spectrum of decreasing human involvement, and it's moving fast. Cloud Code went from 30-second tasks last year to 15-minute autonomous runs today. Auto mode just shipped. Automated testing is coming. Every piece of the loop—planning, implementation, QA—is being internalized by the agent.

The people who understand how agent harnesses work, who know how to use tools like Claude Code to do economically valuable things, are a vanishingly small percentage of the population right now. We're talking sub-1%. And the gap between what that group can produce in a day versus everyone else is already massive and growing.

William Gibson said it best: the future is here, it's just unevenly distributed. You have access to technology right now that lets you do in a day what used to take a team months.

I've sold the exact same system for $500 and $5,000. What changed was my ability to deliver value.

First, I started solving problems that cost more money. I'd get on a call with a marketing agency charging $10K/month and discover they had two needs.

Expense reporting—admin staff manually submitting receipts, accounting team spending 3-4 hours a week categorizing them. That costs them maybe $1,000 a month. Then speed to lead—they're responding to inbound inquiries in 3 hours instead of 5 minutes, and five leads a month are leaking through the funnel. At their conversion rate and contract value, that costs them $30,000 a month. Both take me 3-4 hours to solve with a Make.com workflow. Both use a webhook trigger, some data storage, and a transformation step.

In general, the closer your solution is to revenue generation, the more people will be willing to pay for it.

Second, I stopped just giving people the system and started giving them an experience.

Think about coffee. You can make a cup at home for 30 cents or buy the same cup at a cafe for $6. What's the difference? Certainly not 20x worth of beans and water. It's the smells, the barista, the interior, the Wi-Fi, and the energy. That cafe increased the perceived value by 20x by changing everything about the coffee except the coffee itself.

So instead of just delivering a speed-to-lead system for $3,000, I deliver the same system plus a full environment config, weekly strategy calls, Slack access, Loom documentation, seven additional automation templates, CRM integrations, and a 90-day optimization SOP. I charge $9,000. The extra work is maybe 5 hours on top of the 10 I was already spending. The client thinks they're getting a whole agency relationship.

Third, I just started charging more.

When I was starting LeftClick, I would routinely see people sell the same systems I was selling for $700 for 10 grand. And I would think to myself, how the hell can they sell such a simple system for that much money while I'm here slaving away for a fifteenth of that?

So I took my $1,500 projects and priced them at $4,000. I did not change a single thing about the service—I just got a completely different base of clients. These guys had money and things to do, so incentives insisted they trust my process and give me as much control as possible. Way fewer fixed costs, way less of a pain to deal with, and significantly more upsell opportunity later. You can get away with charging a lot more than you probably think. Most people never stress test it.

document.title: 3 agentic workflows that run my YouTube channel

content:
I just put out a full course on AI agents, and I want to walk you through something from it that I think will change how a lot of you use these tools.

Most people interact with AI agents the same way they interact with ChatGPT. They type a request, get a response, and if it isn't great, they type a slightly different request. But most people are underwhelmed because they treat every session as a blank slate. The agent has no memory of what went wrong last time, accumulated preferences, or learned rules. So it keeps making the same mistakes over and over.

One of the things I cover in the course is self-modifying system prompts. You add a section to your Claude.md or Gemini.md or Agents.md that tells the agent to update its own rules every time you correct it. So if I'm building a website and I say "quit doing things in dark mode," the agent writes a new rule to its own file that says never use dark mode.

By session five or six, the number of errors the agent makes relative to your preferences drops close to zero. Your agent basically trains itself on you over time, and all it cost you was one line of instruction in your system prompt telling it to do so.

That's one technique out of maybe a dozen in the course.

It also covers things like having Claude orchestrate a project while delegating frontend work to Gemini and backend work to Codex simultaneously, spawning 10 agents on the same problem to surface ideas that any single agent would statistically never generate, feeding YouTube tutorials directly into agents so they can learn from video the same way we do, and using fresh agents to review the work of other agents because the original agent is too biased by its own decision history to catch its own mistakes.

The whole course is platform agnostic across Codex, Claude Code, and Antigravity. You don't need any programming experience.

My Instagram has almost 500,000 followers right now. Last month it probably made me around $35,000, which sounds like a lot until you compare it to YouTube. YouTube made me roughly $275,000 in the same period, and I have fewer subscribers on YouTube than I do followers on Instagram.

That's about an 8x difference in revenue with a smaller audience. And the reason is pretty simple—Instagram is a short form platform, and short form platforms just convert way less. You're one swipe away from the next person. It's much harder to build any sort of real relationship with people when they're consuming your content in 15-second increments.

I get a lot of DMs from people in Maker School who are just starting to think about content, and the question is always the same—should I be posting on LinkedIn, X, Instagram, YouTube, TikTok, all of it? And my answer is always no. Pick one platform and go all in on it.

When people try to get into content they try doing everything everywhere all at once. They spin up profiles on 10 different platforms and then they can't maintain the volume necessary to actually succeed on any of them. If you pick one platform, the probability of success on that one platform goes way up because you're actually able to dedicate the time and energy to make things people would consider good.

I also wouldn't recommend shorts. Everybody and their mom can make shorts now—there are talking AI head avatars, fully synthetic content, the supply side is absolutely bonkers. If you throw your hat into the ring on short form right now, the probability you'll be able to stand out in the algorithm is pretty low in my opinion. Long form is what actually converts people into customers, and the revenue difference between a single short form view and a single long form view is staggering.

The reason you see people like me eventually branch out into multiple channels is because YouTube only lets you publish a certain amount of content before your primary subscribers get annoyed. So the play is you have your main channel, you publish as often as your cadence allows, and then you build satellite channels that deal with specific things—daily updates, shorts, unfiltered stuff, whatever. But you don't do that until you're well past 10,000 subscribers on your main thing. 

Before that, you're just spreading yourself too thin.

So if you're just getting started with content right now, here's the roadmap: pick one platform, pick one format, and ride that up to about 10,000 subscribers. Don't experiment with the format or the platform along the way—experiment with the topics until you find one that works. Once you're at 10K, then you can start branching out.

content:
Most people are applying autoresearch to prompts and skills. Great starting point, but the real unlock is realizing this works on anything with a measurable output.

I had an old web app loading in about 1,100 milliseconds. I applied the same autoresearch approach at it: defined load speed as the objective metric, used Google Lighthouse as the measurement tool, let the agent iterate on code changes autonomously. 67 runs later, load time was down to 67 milliseconds. 81.3% improvement. I didn't touch it once.

I'm now running it on my cold email campaigns. The objective metric is reply rate, the measurement tool is my Instantly analytics API, and the agent iterates on the email copy between runs.

The framework is always three ingredients: You need an objective metric, an automated measurement tool so there's no human in the loop slowing things down and you need something the agent can actually modify between runs.

Once you have those three things, you just let it loop. The agent makes a change, measures the result, keeps the winner, tries again over and over until it converges on something significantly better than what you started with.

Every run generates research data—a full log of what the agent tried, what worked, what didn't, and why. When the next generation of models comes out, you hand them the entire history and they pick up where the last one left off. To make a long story short, you're building a compounding asset every time you run this.

content:
My Claude Code skills work about 70% of the time. The other 30% is a bag of rocks.

I wanted to fix that without sitting there rewriting prompts by hand, so I took a concept from Andrej Karpathy's new autoresearch repo and applied it to my own skill library.

The idea is simple. You define a few binary yes/no evaluation criteria for your skill, then you let an agent run the skill dozens of times, score every output, tweak the prompt, and keep the winner.

I tested it on my diagram generator. Four criteria: Is all the text legible? Does it match my pastel color palette? Is the layout linear? Is it free of unnecessary numbering? Max score of 40.

The agent generated 10 diagrams every 2 minutes, evaluated all 10, mutated the prompt, ran again.

Started at 32 out of 40. Hit 39 out of 40 within a handful of runs. That's 97.5%. Total cost was about $10.

One thing I learned fast: keep your evals binary. Yes/no, pass/fail. The moment you introduce scoring scales, you compound variability at every step and your results get noisy. And don't make criteria so narrow the model starts gaming the test instead of actually improving the output. That's the equivalent of a student who doesn't understand the material but still aces the exam.

Everything else gets silently dropped. But the vast majority of use cases people were using it for are now covered by Claude Channels and the Claude Dispatch update that Anthropic dropped a few days earlier. content:
I spent $20.26 and generated 93,000 views. With $100 and the same math, you could be looking at roughly 500,000 views.

There's maybe a 3-6 month window to do this effectively before it gets completely saturated, so I want to explain how it works while it's still worth doing.

There are two technologies intersecting right now that make this possible. The first is AI UGC platforms—tools like Arcads and Higgsfield that let you produce human-level content where the production cost tends towards zero. You can generate realistic talking head videos, screen share content, news breakdowns, whatever format you want, without recording anything yourself.

The second is clipping farms. You treat your content like advertising and then pay other people to distribute it for you. The way it works is you set a campaign on a clipping platform that says something like "if you get me 1,000 views, I'll pay you $2." But the economics are interesting—most of these platforms have view thresholds where the clipper has to hit a certain number of views before they get paid out at all. If they don't hit it, you don't pay. So your effective cost per view ends up being dramatically lower than what you'd expect on paper.

You combine both of these, and you have near-zero production cost with near-zero distribution cost.

The play from there is straightforward. Once you have that distribution you can market products, run affiliates, or build a brand.

document.title: 5 things I wish I knew about automation agencies

content:
I used to spend 5 to 10 hours onboarding every new client at my cold email agency. Now it takes about 90 seconds.

I tell my agentic workflow: "Hey, new client, onboard them." It pulls the sales call transcript, generates a full proposal with personalized problem statements and ROI math, sends a three-part welcome email sequence from different team members, scrapes and enriches leads with the right filters, casualizes every company name so the outreach doesn't read like spam, writes three split-tested cold email campaigns based on our highest performers, sets up an automated reply system with a knowledge base for each campaign, and uploads everything to Instantly ready to send.

All I have to do is a quick QA pass at the end—checking copy, previewing emails, and adjusting any spacing issues.

The way this works is a framework I call DOE—Directive, Orchestration, Execution. You store high-level instructions in plain language files, which are basically your SOPs. You give the agent access to execution scripts it builds itself. And then the orchestration layer figures out how to chain everything together. I don't know how to read most of this code. I don't worry about most of this code. That's the AI's job. The AI is much better at coding than I would ever be, even given a decade of learning.

What's really cool is when something breaks, the workflow just self-heals. During one run, it hit a deprecated API key, found a working one stored somewhere else in my system, updated its own documentation to reference the correct key, and kept going. If I were running a procedural workflow on Make.com or n8n, that would have just errored out. This thing is like Wolverine—it gets shot and the skin comes back.

If you want to do this for your own business, the process is straightforward. Start by compiling your SOPs in natural language. Write them so a monkey could understand them. Send each one to the agent and test it once. AI is only going to get this right maybe 75% of the time the first run, and that's okay. Second time it's 97%. Third time it's 99%. Rinse and repeat across every SOP in your business, then create one meta directive that chains them all together top to bottom.

content:
Scope creep is the single fastest way to turn a profitable project into a money pit.

You quoted $2,500 for a specific set of deliverables. Halfway through the build, the client says "hey, could you also just quickly add..." and suddenly you're doing 40% more work for the same price. Most people eat it because they don't want to damage the relationship.

The fix isn't saying no to clients—it's structuring things upfront so scope creep barely happens in the first place.

I think about client quality as a formula: return divided by the work you put in plus the bullshit you have to deal with. Scope creep destroys both sides of that equation. Your return stays flat while the work and bullshit go through the roof.

Four things I do to prevent it:

Have extraordinarily detailed SOWs. I'm talking line-by-line specifics of what they're getting. Airtable database with this structure, Slack integration that does this, Instantly campaign with this many leads and this many variants. When everything is spelled out, "can you also just..." becomes a much harder ask.

Overdeliver on things that don't take a lot of internal work. A three-page copywriting doc you wrote last year that you just swap the first name on. Loom walkthroughs that double as delivery documentation. Stuff that looks high-value to the client but costs you almost nothing.

Frame everything in terms of ROI from the first call. When the client understands this is a mutually beneficial arrangement and your goal is to get them on a long-term retainer, the whole dynamic shifts.

Explicitly discuss revision requests before the project starts. Outline what a "significant change" looks like so they know you've thought about it. This adds credibility and inoculates you against BS later.

content:
Andrej Karpathy just dropped an open source repo called autoresearch that when you combine it with something like Claude Code becomes self-improving AI.

Karpathy is widely regarded as one of the foremost voices in machine learning. He was a founding member at OpenAI and later head of AI at Tesla. So when he releases something, I pay attention.

The idea is pretty elegant: You give an AI agent a small but real setup and let it experiment autonomously overnight. It modifies something, runs a test, checks if the results improved, keeps or discards the change, and repeats. You wake up in the morning to a log of experiments and hopefully a better outcome than what you started with.

In his case, he was training a machine learning model. The agent would adjust hyperparameters, train for 5 minutes, measure validation loss, and loop. After just a few runs his model got significantly better without him doing anything.

Now I'm not in machine learning. I take models other people have made and use them to make money. But the moment this dropped, I started thinking about ways to apply the same principle to my own business.

To make a long story short, the requirement is simple. You need an objective metric you can track, an API you can call to measure it, and something the agent can modify between runs. If you have those three things, you can build an autonomous experimentation pipeline for almost anything.

I've already set this up for my cold email campaigns. Reply rate is the metric, the Instantly API is the measurement tool, and the agent iterates on the email copy. It runs every hour via GitHub Actions. I'm not even in the loop anymore.

I'm also running it on my Claude Code skills and I used it to take an old web app from 1,100ms load time down to 67ms across 67 autonomous runs.

Landing pages, ad creatives, product descriptions, YouTube titles, pricing pages, chatbot scripts. If you can measure it and an agent can change it, autoresearch applies.
